L27: # Overview of WPF windows
L28: 
L29: Feedback
L30: 
L31: Summarize this article for me
L32: ## In this article
L33: 
L34: Users interact with Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) applications through windows. The primary purpose of a window is to host content that visualizes data and enables users to interact with data. WPF applications provide their own windows by using the 【5†Window】 class. This article introduces 【5†Window】 before covering the fundamentals of creating and managing windows in applications.
L35: 
L36: Important
L37: This article uses XAML generated from a C# project. If you're using Visual Basic, the XAML may look slightly different. These differences are typically present on `x:Class` attribute values. C# includes the root namespace for the project while Visual Basic doesn't.
L38: 
L39: The project templates for C# create an `App` type contained in the app.xaml file. In Visual Basic, the type is named `Application` and the file is named `Application.xaml`.
L40: ## The Window class
L41: 
L42: In WPF, a window is encapsulated by the 【5†Window】 class that you use to do the following:
L43: 
L44:   * Display a window.
L45:   * Configure the size, position, and appearance of a window.
L46:   * Host application-specific content.
L47:   * Manage the lifetime of a window.
L48: 
L49: The following figure illustrates the constituent parts of a window:
L50: 
L51: 【6†Image: Screenshot that shows parts of a WPF window.】
L52: 
L53: A window is divided into two areas: the non-client area and client area.
L54: The non-client area of a window is implemented by WPF and includes the parts of a window that are common to most windows, including the following:
L55: 
L56:   * A title bar (1-5).
L57:   * An icon (1).
L58:   * Title (2).
L59:   * Minimize (3), Maximize (4), and Close (5) buttons.
L60:   * System menu (6) with menu items. Appears when clicking on the icon (1).
L61:   * Border (7).
L62: The client area of a window is the area within a window's non-client area and is used by developers to add application-specific content, such as menu bars, tool bars, and controls.
L63: 
L64:   * Client area (8).
L65:   * Resize grip (9). This is a control added to the Client area (8).
L66: ## Implementing a window
L67: 
L68: The implementation of a typical window includes both appearance and behavior, where appearance defines how a window looks to users and behavior defines the way a window functions as users interact with it. In WPF, you can implement the appearance and behavior of a window using either code or XAML markup.
L69: In general, however, the appearance of a window is implemented using XAML markup, and its behavior is implemented using code-behind, as shown in the following example.
L70: 
L71:     `<Window x:Class="WindowsOverview.Window1"
L72:             xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L73:             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
L74:             xmlns:d="http://schemas.microsoft.com/expression/blend/2008"
L75:             xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006"
L76:             xmlns:local="clr-namespace:WindowsOverview"
L77:             >
L78: 
L79:         <!-- Client area containing the content of the window -->
L80: 
L81:     </Window>
L82:     `
L83: The following code is the code-behind for the XAML.
L84: 
L85:     `using System.Windows;
L86: 
L87:     namespace WindowsOverview
L88:     {
L89:         public partial class Window1 : Window
L90:         {
L91:             public Window1()
L92:             {
L93:                 InitializeComponent();
L94:             }
L95:         }
L96:     }
L97:     `
L98: 
L99:     `Public Class Window1
L100: 
L101:     End Class
L102:     `
L103: 
L104: To enable a XAML markup file and code-behind file to work together, the following are required:
L105:   * In markup, the `Window` element must include the `x:Class` attribute. When the application is built, the existence of `x:Class` attribute causes Microsoft build engine (MSBuild) to generate a `partial` class that derives from 【5†Window】 with the name that is specified by the `x:Class` attribute. This requires the addition of an XML namespace declaration for the XAML schema (`xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"`).
L106: The generated `partial` class implements the `InitializeComponent` method, which is called to register the events and set the properties that are implemented in markup.
L107:   * In code-behind, the class must be a `partial` class with the same name that is specified by the `x:Class` attribute in markup, and it must derive from 【5†Window】. This allows the code-behind file to be associated with the `partial` class that is generated for the markup file when the application is built, for more information, see 【7†Compile a WPF Application】.
L108:   * In code-behind, the 【5†Window】 class must implement a constructor that calls the `InitializeComponent` method. `InitializeComponent` is implemented by the markup file's generated `partial` class to register events and set properties that are defined in markup.
L109: 
L110: Note
L111: When you add a new 【5†Window】 to your project by using Visual Studio, the 【5†Window】 is implemented using both markup and code-behind, and includes the necessary configuration to create the association between the markup and code-behind files as described here.
L112: With this configuration in place, you can focus on defining the appearance of the window in XAML markup and implementing its behavior in code-behind. The following example shows a window with a button that defines an event handler for the 【8†Click】 event. This is implemented in the XAML and the handler is implemented in code-behind.
L113: 
L114:     `<Window x:Class="WindowsOverview.Window1"
L115:             xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
L116:             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
L117:             xmlns:d="http://schemas.microsoft.com/expression/blend/2008"
L118:             xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006"
L119:             xmlns:local="clr-namespace:WindowsOverview"
L120:             >
L121: 
L122:         <!-- Client area containing the content of the window -->
L123: 
L124:         <Button Click="Button_Click">Click This Button</Button>
L125: 
L126:     </Window>
L127:     `
L128: The following code is the code-behind for the XAML.
L129: 
L130:     `using System.Windows;
L131: 
L132:     namespace WindowsOverview
L133:     {
L134:         public partial class Window1 : Window
L135:         {
L136:             public Window1()
L137:             {
L138:                 InitializeComponent();
L139:             }
L140: 
L141:             private void Button_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
L142:             {
L143:                 MessageBox.Show("Button was clicked.");
L144:             }
L145:         }
L146:     }
L147:     `
L148: 
L149:     `Public Class Window1
L150:         Private Sub Button_Click(sender As Object, e As RoutedEventArgs)
L151:             MessageBox.Show("Button was clicked.")
L152:         End Sub
L153: 
L154:     End Class
L155:     `
L156: ### Configuring a window for MSBuild
L157: 
L158: How you implement your window determines how it's configured for MSBuild. For a window that is defined using both XAML markup and code-behind:
L159: 
L160:   * XAML markup files are configured as MSBuild `Page` items.
L161:   * Code-behind files are configured as MSBuild `Compile` items.
L162: .NET SDK projects automatically import the correct `Page` and `Compile` items for you, and you don't need to declare these. When the project is configured for WPF, the XAML markup files are automatically imported as `Page` items, and the corresponding code-behind file is imported as `Compile`.
L163: MSBuild projects won't automatically import the types and you must declare them yourself:
L164: 
L165:     `<Project>
L166:         ...
L167:         <Page Include="MarkupAndCodeBehindWindow.xaml" />
L168:         <Compile Include=" MarkupAndCodeBehindWindow.xaml.cs" />
L169:         ...
L170:     </Project>
L171:     `
L172: 
L173: For information about building WPF applications, see 【7†Compile a WPF Application】.
L174: ## Window lifetime
L175: 
L176: As with any class, a window has a lifetime that begins when it's first instantiated, after which it's opened, activated/deactivated, and eventually closed.

L122: ## Examples
L123: The following example creates a 【17†FileSystemWatcher】 to watch the directory specified at run time. The component is set to watch for changes in `LastWrite` and `LastAccess` time, the creation, deletion, or renaming of text files in the directory. If a file is changed, created, or deleted, the path to the file prints to the console. When a file is renamed, the old and new paths print to the console.
L124: 
L125:     `using System;
L126:     using System.IO;
L127: 
L128:     namespace MyNamespace
L129:     {
L130:         class MyClassCS
L131:         {
L132:             static void Main()
L133:             {
L134:                 using var watcher = new FileSystemWatcher(@"C:\path\to\folder");
L135: 
L136:                 watcher.NotifyFilter = NotifyFilters.Attributes
L137:                                      | NotifyFilters.CreationTime
L138:                                      | NotifyFilters.DirectoryName
L139:                                      | NotifyFilters.FileName
L140:                                      | NotifyFilters.LastAccess
L141:                                      | NotifyFilters.LastWrite
L142:                                      | NotifyFilters.Security
L143:                                      | NotifyFilters.Size;
L144: 
L145:                 watcher.Changed += OnChanged;
L146:                 watcher.Created += OnCreated;
L147:                 watcher.Deleted += OnDeleted;
L148:                 watcher.Renamed += OnRenamed;
L149:                 watcher.Error += OnError;
L150: 
L151:                 watcher.Filter = "*.txt";
L152:                 watcher.IncludeSubdirectories = true;
L153:                 watcher.EnableRaisingEvents = true;
L154: 
L155:                 Console.WriteLine("Press enter to exit.");
L156:                 Console.ReadLine();
L157:             }
L158: 
L159:             private static void OnChanged(object sender, FileSystemEventArgs e)
L160:             {
L161:                 if (e.ChangeType != WatcherChangeTypes.Changed)
L162:                 {
L163:                     return;
L164:                 }
L165:                 Console.WriteLine($"Changed: {e.FullPath}");
L166:             }
L167: 
L168:             private static void OnCreated(object sender, FileSystemEventArgs e)
L169:             {
L170:                 string value = $"Created: {e.FullPath}";
L171:                 Console.WriteLine(value);
L172:             }
L173: 
L174:             private static void OnDeleted(object sender, FileSystemEventArgs e) =>
L175:                 Console.WriteLine($"Deleted: {e.FullPath}");
L176: 
L177:             private static void OnRenamed(object sender, RenamedEventArgs e)
L178:             {
L179:                 Console.WriteLine($"Renamed:");
L180:                 Console.WriteLine($"    Old: {e.OldFullPath}");
L181:                 Console.WriteLine($"    New: {e.FullPath}");
L182:             }

L185:                 PrintException(e.GetException());

L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: SQLite can back up database files while the app is running. This functionality is available in Microsoft.Data.Sqlite as the 【5†BackupDatabase】 method on `SqliteConnection`.
L32: 
L33:     `// Create a full backup of the database
L34:     var backup = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=BackupSample.db");
L35:     connection.BackupDatabase(backup);
L36:     `
L37: Currently, `BackupDatabase` will back up the database as quickly as possible and blocks other connections from writing to the database. Issue 【6†#13834†github.com】 would provide an alternative API to back up the database in the background and allow other connections to interrupt the backup and write to the database. If you're interested, provide feedback on the issue.
